findings.title: Backup code consumption is not atomic (read-modify-write race)
findings.body: The authorize callback decrypts the backup code list, checks membership with indexOf, then nulls the used entry and writes the whole list back with prisma.user.update. Two concurrent login requests using the same backup code can both read the list before either writes, both pass the indexOf check, and both be accepted — a single backup code can be replayed. The update should be conditioned on the code still being present (e.g. compare-and-swap or a transaction with a where guard) so a code can only be redeemed once.

findings.title: "missing_backup_codes" message tells users to regenerate codes in settings, but no such feature exists
findings.body: The new error string is "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." This PR adds no UI or API to view or regenerate backup codes after setup — codes are generated once during initial 2FA setup and (after use of one) can never be replenished. A user who exhausts or loses their codes is told to do something impossible. Either a regenerate feature must be added or the message must be corrected.

findings.title: Backup codes are generated and persisted before 2FA is actually enabled
findings.body: The setup endpoint (which only requires the account password) writes encrypted backupCodes to the user row and returns the plaintext codes in the response, even though twoFactorEnabled is still false at this point. If the user abandons the wizard after the password step (or the QR/secret display step) and never calls enable, valid backup codes remain stored and were transmitted to the client. Any later flow that treats the presence of backupCodes as meaningful (e.g. the MissingBackupCodes vs. present-codes distinction in login) operates on codes the user may never have seen or saved. Generating codes only on successful enable (or clearing them if setup is abandoned) would be safer.

findings.title: Dismissing the modal at the DisplayBackupCodes step never calls onEnable, leaving the UI switch stale
findings.body: After enable succeeds the modal moves to SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes, and only the explicit Close button calls onEnable(). If the user closes the dialog via the X button, Escape, or the overlay (all handled by onOpenChange, not resetState/onEnable), two-factor is now actually enabled server-side but the parent's onEnable callback never fires, so the settings page keeps showing 2FA as disabled until reload. resetState() is also skipped, so stale backup codes/blob URL remain in component state.

findings.title: No test covers actually logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
findings.body: The PR's core feature — authenticating with a backup code — has zero test coverage. The e2e additions only exercise the download/copy/close buttons on the backup-code display screen; the file even carries a TODO ("add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup") and the download-content/clipboard checks are TODOs. The server-side redemption logic in next-auth-options.ts and disable.ts (dash stripping, single-use invalidation, MissingBackupCodes/IncorrectBackupCode paths) is untested, so a regression in the only code path that verifies backup codes would go unnoticed.

findings.title: Backup code is consumed even if login subsequently fails
findings.body: The used backup code is nulled and persisted in the database immediately after the indexOf match, before the rest of the authorize function runs (team checks, password-policy role validation, JWT/session creation). If anything after that point throws or the sign-in callback redirects (e.g. an INACTIVE_ADMIN downgrade or an error during token issuance), the user has permanently lost a backup code without gaining access. The invalidation should be tied to successful sign-in, not to passing the code check.

findings.title: minLength/maxLength/required on the backup code input are not enforced on the login form
findings.body: The login form in apps/web/pages/auth/login.tsx is rendered with noValidate, so the native minLength={10}/maxLength={11}/required attributes on the BackupCode TextField never trigger. The zod schema also does not include backupCode (the object is .passthrough()), so a user can submit an empty or malformed backup code; the empty string is falsy on the server, so the request silently falls into the TOTP branch and returns a confusing "second factor required" error instead of a validation message telling the user to enter the code.
